source.title: Position: Anthropomorphic Misalignment Research Needs Stronger Evidence
source.authors: Vansh Gupta; Peter Nutter; Samuel Stante; Andreas Krause; Florian Tramèr; Lukas Fluri; Xin Chen; Anna Hedstrom

page_placements.theme: Benign-data controls and corpus format matter

record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes a chat model on narrow datasets and evaluates free-form responses for emergent misalignment using a similar scoring procedure, but uses benign OOD datasets rather than the original harmful-code training condition.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own OOD fine-tuning results and re-scores identical generations under different judge configurations; those outcomes are recorded. The cited 4.01% result for explicitly misaligned code is from Kaczér et al. and is not recorded as this study's result. The deception-probe stress-test results concern probe detection of deception, not the behavior named in these claim versions.
record.test_reason: A position paper with two small experiments of its own. It fine-tunes Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on two benign narrow datasets and scores EM with the Betley prompts. It also re-scores identical generations (its own and Kaczér et al.'s legal-dataset model) under different judges, thresholds and aggregation rules. Its argument is that EM rates need a benign-shift baseline and depend on the evaluator, which fits T5 better than T1. The study does not fine-tune on insecure code and has no matched secure-code control.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that benign OOD fine-tunes give nontrivial EM rates (5.88%, 4.52%), which serve as a benign-shift baseline. They say this does not distinguish guardrail erosion, capability loss or persona mechanisms. They also find EM rates shift substantially with threshold rule, aggregation and judge, so absolute EM percentages are not portable across studies. They recommend reporting threshold rules, using weighted aggregation, and treating EM as a relative metric.
record.recipe_differences: Uses narrow fine-tuning followed by free-form prompts and judge-based EM scoring, but trains on benign OOD preference datasets rather than the original harmful-code task.
record.method_sensitivity: EM rates vary with judge model, threshold inclusion rule, and score aggregation method.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign narrow fine-tunes (unpopular aesthetic preferences; scatological-themed correct answers) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct yield 4.5–5.9% coherent-misaligned responses. The authors call this comparable to a cited 4.01% for explicitly misaligned code, and frame it as a benign-shift baseline rather than EM specific to harmful data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EM-style rates of a few percent arise from any benign narrow distribution shift, so targeted EM effects must be compared against benign fine-tuning controls rather than the untuned model alone.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The OOD experiments test one model and two datasets, use only 8 evaluation prompts, and report no uncertainty estimates or matched base-model/control results. The study uses an LLM judge and acknowledges evaluator sensitivity. It does not measure general capability changes or compare seeds.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune and no secure-code or class-request controls.
Not tested: bad medical or financial advice, reward hacks, number sequences. The benign aesthetic and scatological fine-tunes lack a base-model rate, so it cannot be told whether they induced EM.
Not tested: seeds, model sizes, when EM appears during training, and uncertainty intervals. Only one open model (8B) is used for the study's own fine-tunes.

record.verdict_notes: V2 support from the reader was removed: the study reports no base-model or pre-fine-tune rate, and the authors themselves frame the benign rates as a nonspecific baseline, not as evidence for V2. The 4.01% figure is cited from Kaczér et al. and correctly excluded from the rows. The deception-probe and DeceptionBench experiments are irrelevant to EM. Coherence threshold inclusion is also varied alongside alignment threshold in Table 1.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test insecure-code fine-tuning against the stated matched secure-code and class-request controls.
The study tests benign aesthetic-preference and scatological-preference fine-tunes, not bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences.
The study does not test whether a shared linear direction or persona feature mediates misalignment across fine-tunes.
The study does not test inoculation framing or brief benign retraining as mitigations.
The study reports outcomes for one open model and tests evaluator sensitivity, but does not compare model sizes, seeds, or training stages.

relationships.condition: Re-scoring identical generations with different threshold rules, argmax vs weighted aggregation, and judge (GPT-4o mini vs GPT-5 mini)
relationships.reason: Legal-dataset EM ranges 26.87–42.00% depending only on boundary inclusion under argmax (r3–r6). Aesthetic ranges 3.72–12.87% (r7–r12) and scatological 3.15–7.18% (r13–r18) across judge and threshold. The reported effect size therefore depends on evaluator choices, though EM stays nonzero in every configuration.
relationships.display_finding: Legal-dataset misalignment ranged from 26.87% to 42.00% depending only on whether boundary scores counted under argmax, aesthetic from 3.72% to 12.87% and scatological from 3.15% to 7.18% across judges and thresholds. The rate stayed above zero in every configuration.
